summary: We are testing whether a circular-buffer rotation sort algorithm can optimally solve problem #15 (prefix-suffix swap sorting) in ≤2n+1 operations, achieving a perfect score of 100, versus a no-operation baseline that should score 0. This validates that the specific algorithmic mechanism—not a trivial problem property—drives the score.
key_points: h-main: A 3-phase algorithm places elements 1..n into sorted order using at most 2n+1 operations (≤2001 for n=1000, well under the 4n=4000 limit). It exploits the prefix-suffix swap as a circular rotation on the unsorted buffer. Probe data on 50 random permutations averaged 1985 ops. Prediction: score = 100 on all test cases.

h-control-negative: Outputs 0 operations, leaving the permutation unsorted. The checker requires a fully sorted result, so this should score 0. If it scores >0, something is wrong with our understanding of the judge.

Confirmation criteria: h-main scores 100 (or very close) AND h-control scores 0. Refutation: h-main scores <100 would indicate the algorithm doesn't always produce a fully sorted permutation or uses too many ops; h-control scoring >0 would indicate the judge doesn't require sorting.

The scoring formula is 100 × clamp((4n − our_ops) / (4n − best_ops), 0, 1). With best_ops likely ≈2001 and our algorithm at ≈2001, we expect near-perfect scores. The key risk is edge cases (element already in place, last-2-element endgame) which the code handles with explicit special cases.
Each arm requires one judge call (~30-60s). Total experiment time: ~2 minutes. No unlocked parameters affect the algorithmic outcome; compiler flags and C++ standard are standard choices.
